html:
The Longmen Grottoes are cave temples carved into the limestone cliffs on both banks of the Yi River, south of Luoyang in central China. They hold tens of thousands of Buddhist statues, carved over some four centuries, and are among the finest works of Chinese Buddhist art.

Work began around 493, when Emperor Xiaowen of the Northern Wei (Toba Wei) moved his capital to Luoyang. His court had already carved the Yungang Grottoes near the old capital. The early Longmen figures are slender and elegant, in long, flowing robes.

A second great phase came under the Tang. Its masterpiece is the giant seated Vairocana Buddha of Fengxian Temple, about 17 metres tall, finished in 675. Wu Zetian, then empress, gave money for it, and some say its calm face was modelled on hers. Carving slowed after the Tang persecution of Buddhism in the 840s. Many heads were later cut off and sold abroad. Longmen became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.
